Title: Random forest snow-to-liquid ratio algorithm for the contiguous United States
Brief Abstract: This repository contains code associated with the manuscript "Snow-to-liquid ratio prediction over the contiguous United States using machine learning" (Pletcher et al., in press / published in Weather and Forecasting, AMS journal, around 2025-2026). It implements machine learning models-primarily random forests (with some linear regression baselines)-to predict snow-to-liquid ratio (SLR) across the contiguous United States (CONUS). SLR is the ratio of snowfall depth to liquid-equivalent precipitation, crucial for accurate snowfall accumulation forecasts (snowfall = liquid precip  SLR). The models use a CONUS-wide training dataset pairing CoCoRaHS (Community Collaborative Rain, Hail and Snow Network) snowfall observations with ERA5 reanalysis profiles. They outperform traditional National Weather Service (NWS) SLR methods and can be applied to any weather modeling system (e.g., HRRR, NBM). Key features include training/validation scripts, prediction on point profiles or 3-D grids, post-processing, and examples for operational forecast integration. It builds on earlier efforts (linked to a prior repo) and focuses on improving winter weather hazard prediction (e.g., heavy snow events, travel/avalanche risks). The code supports data download, profile pairing, model training, and inference.

Title: "Can AI forecast if snow will be fluffy or dense? Only with help from humans" (Focusing on machine learning models for forecasting the Snow-to-Liquid Ratio)
Brief Abstract: This is an in-depth journalistic article detailing how researchers are utilizing machine learning (artificial intelligence) to better forecast the Snow-to-Liquid Ratio (SLR)-the metric that determines whether a winter storm will yield dense, heavy snow or light, fluffy powder. Historically governed by a generic "10-to-1" rule of thumb, accurate SLR prediction remains notoriously difficult. The article highlights two recent scientific studies (including a January 2026 paper published in Weather and Forecasting) that trained computer models using decades of meticulously hand-collected snow data from across the United States. The resulting AI algorithms significantly outperform traditional methods by analyzing complex ambient atmospheric variables like temperature and wind speed, offering a major breakthrough for meteorologists, winter storm planners, and water resource managers.

Title: Spatial Aligned Mean: A Method to Improve Consensus Forecasts of Precipitation from Convection-Allowing Model Ensembles
Brief Abstract: Ensembles of convection-allowing model (CAM) forecasts are increasingly being used in operational numerical weather forecasting. Several approaches have been devised to find consensus among ensemble forecast fields, including the arithmetic ensemble mean and, more recently, the patchwise localized probability-matched (LPM) mean. However, differences in spatial distribution and intensity of precipitation features among ensemble members make it difficult to construct an ensemble mean product that characterizes the consensus while preserving precipitation structures forecasted by the individual ensemble members. To overcome this problem, this study aims to develop and test a method for improving ensemble consensus precipitation forecasts by directly considering the spatial offsets among ensemble members. This study uses a multiscale spatial alignment technique to align the precipitation features of each ensemble member to a common location, and the spatial aligned mean (SAM) is obtained by averaging the realigned members. It is shown that implementing SAM and subsequently applying the LPM technique to the average of all aligned members (SAM-LPM) can significantly improve the warm season precipitation forecast scores using common metrics such as equitable threat score (ETS). Also, improvement in the structure of features of heavy rainfall is shown from summer 2023 flash-flooding cases. Thus, SAM and SAM-LPM can be excellent candidate methods for calculating an ensemble consensus and providing ensemble consensus guidance to forecasters.

Title: Evaluation of an Experimental 15-Member FV3-LAM Ensemble for the Summer 2024 Flash Flood and Intense Rainfall Experiment
Brief Abstract: A 15-member experimental ensemble using the Finite-Volume Cubed-Sphere Limited Area Model (FV3-LAM) dynamic core is evaluated for precipitation forecasting during summer 2024. The ensemble was run once daily out to an 84-h lead, for a total of 30 days, in support of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) Hydrometeorological Testbed's Flash Flood and Intense Rainfall Experiment. It employs a variety of physics combinations, boundary conditions, radar data assimilation, and cumulus convective schemes. Evaluation via contingency table metrics suggests that activating cumulus convective schemes, in conjunction with Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) boundary conditions, may have a detrimental effect on precipitation forecasts beyond day 1. Additionally, greater biases are noted in members using the Noah-MP land surface scheme than in others. Radar reflectivity data assimilation improves ensemble performance on day 1, while a realignment of features to a common position among members (spatial aligned mean) improves the performance of ensemble consensus products. An experimental Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) member run alongside the FV3 ensemble shows competitive performance out to day 2, with slightly worse performance during days 3 and 4. The results helped inform ongoing Rapid Refresh Forecasting System (RRFS) development during and after the experiment. Recommendations based on these results are subsequently made for future model development and forecast experiments.

Title: CAPS HWT/HMT Ensemble Viewer
Brief Abstract: The website, maintained by the Center for Analysis and Prediction of Storms (CAPS) at the University of Oklahoma, provides real-time weather forecast visualizations. It features "postage stamp" displays of various meteorological data, including 2-meter above-ground level (AGL) temperature, wind, simulated radar, composite reflectivity, precipitation types (including mixed precipitation), and quantitative precipitation forecasts (QPF) for 1, 3, 6, and 24-hour periods. Additionally, it includes snowfall forecasts for similar timeframes and machine learning (U-net) products for rainfall and snowfall predictions, such as ensemble means and thresholds (e.g., >0.5", >1.0"). The site offers interactive controls like play/pause, navigation through forecast times, and keyboard shortcuts for user convenience.

Title: CSU-MLP (Colorado State University Machine Learning Probabilities) - Precipitation & Excessive Rainfall Forecasts
Brief Abstract: The CSU-MLP system is a post-processing framework that uses Random Forest machine learning algorithms to predict the probability of hazardous weather-specifically Excessive Rainfall (QPF) and severe convective hazards (hail, wind, tornadoes). The system works by taking large-scale environmental data from the Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) and the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) and comparing them to a historical database of past weather events. It identifies patterns that previously led to extreme rain or flash floods to produce a "first-guess" probabilistic map. These maps are used daily by forecasters at the NOAA Weather Prediction Center (WPC) to help issue official national Excessive Rainfall Outlooks.

Title: Quantification of Precipitation Asymmetries of Tropical Cyclones Using 16-Year TRMM Observations
Brief Abstract: Both low and higher wavenumber asymmetries of tropical cyclone (TC) precipitation are quantified from 16 years of Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) microwave imager rainfall estimates using Fourier decomposition. The energy spectrum of rainfall perturbation and impacts of the storm motion and vertical wind shear to the rainfall asymmetry are analyzed. It is found that the wavenumber 1 perturbation only contributes 37% of the total perturbation energy of total TC precipitation, while over 70% of the total perturbation energy is from the sum of wavenumbers 1 through 6. Most of the total precipitation asymmetry is from the heavy precipitation, and contributions for light and moderate precipitation types are small. The maximum motion-relative precipitation asymmetry is generally located down motion but shifts cyclonically after adding wavenumber 2-6 components to wavenumber 1. The asymmetry index of wavenumber 1 and 1-6 asymmetries relative to the vertical wind shear is about 2 to 3 times as large as that relative to the storm motion. The vertical wind shear is a more important factor than the storm motion in producing precipitation asymmetry, especially for the wavenumber 1. A dominant downshear left wavenumber-1 asymmetry maximum is found regardless of the shear vector orientation to the TC motion, the magnitude of the shear value, and the speed of TC motion. However, the maximum asymmetry of wavenumber 1-6 asymmetry becomes downshear right for the subgroup with low shear, fast motion, and the shear vector left to the motion.

Title: Classifying Precipitation Types in Tropical Cyclones Using the NRL 37 GHz Color Product
Brief Abstract: The tropical cyclone (TC) webpage developed by the U.S. Naval Research Lab (NRL) has been widely used by the community for realtime TC monitoring and forecasting. Using 14 years of Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission Microwave Imager and Precipitation Radar data in TCs, precipitation/convection types are quantitatively classified based on vertical radar profiles corresponding to seven different color regions in the NRL's 37 GHz color composite product. The bright cyan and all pink (including pure pink, bright cyan/pink, and weak cyan/pink, and green/pink) regions are identified as nearly 100% precipitative regions. The bright cyan and pure pink regions are shallow and deep convective precipitation, respectively, while the green/pink, weak cyan/pink, and bright cyan/pink regions are mainly stratiform rain. Eightyfour percent of pixels in the weak cyan region are precipitating, including either shallow convective, stratiform, or anvil precipitation. Seventysix percent of pixels in the green region are nonprecipitating pixels, and 24% of them are very lightly precipitating pixels, which could be contaminated from clouds with high liquid water content. The ability to perform TC precipitationtype analysis of this detail (convective versus stratiform and deep versus shallow) was previously only possible using radarbased classification algorithms. Using the 37 GHz precipitationtype analysis, a significant increase of coverage of stratiform precipitation and shallow convection in the inner core is found between 3 and 21 hr before the onset of TC rapid intensification.
